plan.scene: In a busy square just inside the gate of a walled ancient town, in clear morning sunlight that is turning toward midday, townsfolk in plain tunics, cloaks and shawls pass along the stone streets, carrying baskets of goods and talking as merchants call out at their stalls. Where the crossroads meet beside the open gateway, a soft radiance and drifting golden light spread through the air above the paths, as if the light itself were gathering and settling over the crowd without any shape or form to be seen. Some of the passersby pause and turn their faces toward the glow with quiet attention, while a merchant opens a storeroom door on the square to reveal stacked jars and sacks, the light falling warmly across the goods and the stone threshold. The streets and gates are the main setting, with the crowd and the market goods showing the plenty that the light brings to those who seek it.

plan.scene: In the still, cool night beside a Persian royal palace, a deep circular pit of dressed grey limestone lies at the foot of the palace court, its mouth open to the sky. Torchlight and lamplight fall across the stone rim while a heavy stone slab is lowered by bronze-fitted ropes and set squarely over the opening. King Darius, in a dark Persian court robe and mantle, stands at the rim with his gold signet ring pressed into a softened clay seal on the slab's edge, and beside him a few lords in court robes lean in to press their own rings into the same seal. Daniel, in a plain Israelite tunic and cloak, stands at the far edge of the rim in quiet composure, his hands loosely held before him and his face turned down toward the dark. Within the pit, dim firelight glows faintly far below the stone, suggesting the lions' presence without showing them. Cool air moves softly through the court, the torches flicker, and the wide stillness of the night presses over the scene.

plan.scene: Under pale dawn light before the sun clears the ridge, a priest in plain undyed linen tunic of ochre-cream stands at the bronze altar of burnt offering in the open court before the portable tabernacle, its linen hangings stirring slightly in the still air. He bends to the east side of the altar, where he sets aside the crop and feathers of a dove, the small bundled remains lying on the sand in the place of the ashes, which lie grey and cool beside the stone base. A thin column of smoke rises from the fire on the altar, and a faint glow of fire lingers in its hearth, while cloud-radiance hangs softly over the tabernacle roof. Behind the court, Moses in an earth-brown wool cloak stands with his hands at his sides, attentive to the priestly work, and beyond him Israelite men and women in woven tunics and dusty cloaks gather quietly among their tents spread across the sand, watching in grave stillness. The clear desert air holds a faint dry breeze, and the scene carries a sense of solemn order and quiet dignity.

plan.scene: In the late afternoon light of Jerusalem, a weary figure of a man in plain undyed wool, sandals dusty, leans against a rough stone wall of the city, one hand pressed to the stone for support while his head lifts slightly toward the pale sky. Nearby, a few townsfolk in plain tunics and cloaks pause at the edge of a dusty lane, their shoulders bowed from labor, some setting down jars of water, and a child grips a parent's cloak. The warm low sun falls across the stone houses and temple court beyond, casting long soft shadows over the dust, while high pale cloud drifts overhead and a gentle radiance, like light through cloud rather than any human form, rests on the weary figure, suggesting strength flowing into his frame. The mood is quiet and hopeful, grounded in the ordinary exhaustion of daily life and the sudden steadying of those who had no might left.

plan.scene: Late afternoon in Corinth, the low golden sun slanting across a quiet stone colonnade at the city's edge, a bronze mirror lying tilted on a low stone ledge in the foreground, its polished surface catching a faint blur of light and reflecting only dim, wavering shapes of the colonnade's columns. Beyond the columns, the marketplace stalls are closing as merchants fold their awnings, and a few Roman soldiers in military dress move slowly near the city gate in the distance, their outlines softened by the warm haze. A light breeze stirs the dust and lifts a loose edge of a drawn cloak on a passing figure in the mid-ground, a Corinthian believer walking away from the viewer. The sky above is clear and pale gold, deepening toward dusk at the top of the frame, and the long shadows of the columns stretch across the paving stones toward the viewer. No figure looks into the mirror; it is left to show the dim, partial sight of which the words speak, while the wider city stands ready in full light beyond it.

moment.text: Turn, and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all the places near there: in the Arabah, in the hill country, in the lowland, in the South, by the seashore, in the land of the Canaanites, and in Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates.

next.text: Behold, I have set the land before you. Go in and possess the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers—to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob—to give to them and to their offspring after them.’”

plan.scene: At dawn near Horeb, Moses stands on a rise of stony ground in woven wool cloak, one arm lifted toward the open country ahead, while the Israelite people in simple woven tunics gather their tent poles, staves and water skins beside their camp. Their figures are arranged in loose groups, some already turning their faces south and east, as the desert light grows bright over the hills. Above the ridges a pale column of cloud and a spread of fire-glow rest across the high ground, marking God's presence in the place without any form. Beyond the valley the Arabah and lowlands fall away in pale heat haze toward the South and the far hill country, with dust lifting from the dry earth and the distant line of the great river only faintly visible on the horizon. Bronze tools, bundled tent cloth and scattered stones lie along the track, and the mood is one of grounded resolve as the people turn to take up the journey.

plan.scene: In the bright late-morning sun of Jerusalem, a stretch of rubble-strewn city wall rises in fresh courses of pale stone near the gateway area. Rephaiah, a sturdy man in a dust-stained working tunic and head covering, stands on a low pile of stones, bending to set a large dressed block into place while two companions in sweat-worn cloaks steady it with ropes and wooden levers. Behind him, workers carry baskets of rubble and mortar along a path cut through debris, and a few laborers in tunics pause to wipe their brows. Long soft shadows from the south stretch across the new masonry, and the wide wall runs off into the haze toward the distant gate, its restored sections catching warm light while older broken stretches remain dark and uneven. The air feels dry and warm under a clear sky, and the scene is calm and purposeful, showing ordinary dignity in shared labor.

plan.scene: In the wilderness of Sinai, under clear dry desert light, the portable tabernacle stands at the center of the Israelite encampment, its linen-covered frame and curtains catching the sun. A still column of luminous cloud rests over its roof, not moving, a soft radiance rather than a storm. Around it, tents of woven goat-hair cloth are pitched in orderly rows, and the people sit or stand quietly beside their tent doors, some tending bedding, some resting in their simple tunics and travel wraps, their faces calm and patient as they wait. A few families sit in the shade of their tents, children playing quietly nearby, while a small group of priests in white linen garments stands near the tabernacle entrance, watching the cloud. Packed donkeys and folded tent coverings lie ready beside the tents but remain unloaded, showing that the camp has chosen to stay. Dust lies still on the ground, and the scene holds an atmosphere of reverent stillness and steady trust.

moment.text: “Whose house is it?” “Dr. Becher’s.” “Tell me,” broke in the engineer, “is Dr. Becher a German, very thin, with a long, sharp nose?” The station-master laughed heartily. “No, sir, Dr. Becher is an Englishman, and there isn’t a man in the parish who has a better-lined waistcoat. But he has a gentleman staying with him, a patient, as I understand, who is a foreigner, and he looks as if a little good Berkshire beef would do him no harm.” The station-master had not finished his speech before we were all hastening in the direction of the fire. The road topped a low hill, and there was a great widespread whitewashed building in front of us, spouting fire at every chink and window, while in the garden in front three fire-engines were vainly striving to keep the flames under.

plan.scene: Late at night on a rural Berkshire lane, the four men crest a low hill and stop short, hats and wool overcoats silhouetted against a sky blazing orange. Below them the great whitewashed country house at Eyford spouts flame from every window and chink, smoke drifting low across the cold, clear air. In the garden in front, three brass fire-engines stand on the wet grass, their crews in plain work clothes pumping and dousing vainly at the fire, water arcing and steaming in the glow. The station-master, a stocky Englishman in a buttoned waistcoat and overcoat, stands half-turned toward the group, his face lit by the flickering light. Holmes, tall and lean in a dark greatcoat, leans forward with quiet attention, while Watson steadies his hat beside him. Victor Hatherley, pale and tense in his overcoat, stares fixedly down toward the gravel drive, and Inspector Bradstreet, in his dark official coat, watches the crowd of villagers gathering at the gate. The orange light glints on the gravel, the rose-bushes and the dark windows of the house, and the scene is filled with the roar of fire and the sharp smell of smoke.

moment.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle ¶71 to The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle ¶78
moment.text: When the commissionaire had gone, Holmes took up the stone and held it against the light. “It’s a bonny thing,” said he. “Just see how it glints and sparkles. Of course it is a nucleus and focus of crime. Every good stone is. They are the devil’s pet baits. In the larger and older jewels every facet may stand for a bloody deed. This stone is not yet twenty years old. It was found in the banks of the Amoy River in southern China and is remarkable in having every characteristic of the carbuncle, save that it is blue in shade instead of ruby red. In spite of its youth, it has already a sinister history. There have been two murders, a vitriol-throwing, a suicide, and several robberies brought about for the sake of this forty-grain weight of crystallised charcoal. Who would think that so pretty a toy would be a purveyor to the gallows and the prison? I’ll lock it up in my strong box now and drop a line to the Countess to say that we have it.” “Do you think that this man Horner is innocent?” “I cannot tell.” “Well, then, do you imagine that this other one, Henry Baker, had anything to do with the matter?” “It is, I think, much more likely that Henry Baker is an absolutely innocent man, who had no idea that the bird which he was carrying was of considerably more value than if it were made of solid gold. That, however, I shall determine by a very simple test if we have an answer to our advertisement.” “And you can do nothing until then?” “Nothing.” “In that case I shall continue my professional round. But I shall come back in the evening at the hour you have mentioned, for I should like to see the solution of so tangled a business.”

moment.reference: A Case of Identity ¶92 to A Case of Identity ¶101
moment.text: I held the little printed slip to the light. “Missing,” it said, “on the morning of the fourteenth, a gentleman named Hosmer Angel. About five ft. seven in. in height; strongly built, sallow complexion, black hair, a little bald in the centre, bushy, black side-whiskers and moustache; tinted glasses, slight infirmity of speech. Was dressed, when last seen, in black frock-coat faced with silk, black waistcoat, gold Albert chain, and grey Harris tweed trousers, with brown gaiters over elastic-sided boots. Known to have been employed in an office in Leadenhall Street. Anybody bringing,” &c, &c. “That will do,” said Holmes. “As to the letters,” he continued, glancing over them, “they are very commonplace. Absolutely no clue in them to Mr. Angel, save that he quotes Balzac once. There is one remarkable point, however, which will no doubt strike you.” “They are typewritten,” I remarked. “Not only that, but the signature is typewritten. Look at the neat little ‘Hosmer Angel’ at the bottom. There is a date, you see, but no superscription except Leadenhall Street, which is rather vague. The point about the signature is very suggestive—in fact, we may call it conclusive.” “Of what?” “My dear fellow, is it possible you do not see how strongly it bears upon the case?” “I cannot say that I do unless it were that he wished to be able to deny his signature if an action for breach of promise were instituted.” “No, that was not the point. However, I shall write two letters, which should settle the matter. One is to a firm in the City, the other is to the young lady’s stepfather, Mr. Windibank, asking him whether he could meet us here at six o’clock to-morrow evening. It is just as well that we should do business with the male relatives. And now, Doctor, we can do nothing until the answers to those letters come, so we may put our little problem upon the shelf for the interim.” I had had so many reasons to believe in my friend’s subtle powers of reasoning and extraordinary energy in action that I felt that he must have some solid grounds for the assured and easy demeanour with which he treated the singular mystery which he had been called upon to fathom. Once only had I known him to fail, in the case of the King of Bohemia and of the Irene Adler photograph; but when I looked back to the weird business of the Sign of Four, and the extraordinary circumstances connected with the Study in Scarlet, I felt that it would be a strange tangle indeed which he could not unravel. I left him then, still puffing at his black clay pipe, with the conviction that when I came again on the next evening I would find that he held in his hands all the clues which would lead up to the identity of the disappearing bridegroom of Miss Mary Sutherland.

previous.text: “I noted, in passing, that she had written a note before leaving home but after being fully dressed. You observed that her right glove was torn at the forefinger, but you did not apparently see that both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning, or the mark would not remain clear upon the finger. All this is amusing, though rather elementary, but I must go back to business, Watson. Would you mind reading me the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel?”

moment.text: There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it: a Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and the other two were using it as a cushion, resting their elbows on it, and talking over its head. “Very uncomfortable for the Dormouse,” thought Alice; “only, as it’s asleep, I suppose it doesn’t mind.” The table was a large one, but the three were all crowded together at one corner of it: “No room! No room!” they cried out when they saw Alice coming. “There’s _plenty_ of room!” said Alice indignantly, and she sat down in a large arm-chair at one end of the table. “Have some wine,” the March Hare said in an encouraging tone. Alice looked all round the table, but there was nothing on it but tea. “I don’t see any wine,” she remarked. “There isn’t any,” said the March Hare. “Then it wasn’t very civil of you to offer it,” said Alice angrily.

moment.reference: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground ¶41 to The Queen’s Croquet-Ground ¶44
moment.text: “Get to your places!” shouted the Queen in a voice of thunder, and people began running about in all directions, tumbling up against each other; however, they got settled down in a minute or two, and the game began. Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her life; it was all ridges and furrows; the balls were live hedgehogs, the mallets live flamingoes, and the soldiers had to double themselves up and to stand on their hands and feet, to make the arches. The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo: she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it _would_ twist itself round and look up in her face, with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing: and when she had got its head down, and was going to begin again, it was very provoking to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself, and was in the act of crawling away: besides all this, there was generally a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog to, and, as the doubled-up soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon came to the conclusion that it was a very difficult game indeed. The players all played at once without waiting for turns, quarrelling all the while, and fighting for the hedgehogs; and in a very short time the Queen was in a furious passion, and went stamping about, and shouting “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” about once in a minute. Alice began to feel very uneasy: to be sure, she had not as yet had any dispute with the Queen, but she knew that it might happen any minute, “and then,” thought she, “what would become of me? They’re dreadfully fond of beheading people here; the great wonder is, that there’s any one left alive!”

plan.scene: On the Queen's croquet-ground, a ridged and furrowed lawn under a flat, overcast afternoon sky with soft, even daylight, Alice stands mid-game in her Victorian child's dress and white pinafore, clutching a live flamingo tucked under one arm with its long legs dangling down. The flamingo has its neck half-straightened and its head twisted round to gaze up into Alice's face with a puzzled expression, and Alice is caught half-laughing as she tries to steady it. Nearby, a hedgehog has unrolled itself and is crawling away across a furrow, another ball lost to the ground. Flat, oblong playing-card soldiers, with heads, arms and legs, are doubled over with their hands and feet planted to form arches, while others hurry off across the lawn in different directions. In the background the courtiers and players, in period robes, waistcoats and hats, mill about in a crowd, and the Queen of Hearts, in the distance, stamps and shouts, her furious gesture a blur of threat rather than harm.

moment.text: The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice. “Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar. plan.scene: In a dim Wonderland wood on a still, warm late afternoon, a great toadstool rises in a clearing among tall grass, its caps tinged with a dreamy greenish glow. Soft dappled sunlight filters through the trees, and a faint haze of hookah smoke drifts in the still air. The Caterpillar sits atop the mushroom, a large blue-green caterpillar with a period waistcoat and a small hat, its long hookah pipe held in one hand and drawn away from its mouth as it turns its sleepy, sidelong gaze toward Alice. Alice stands on the grass at the foot of the toadstool in her Victorian child's dress and white pinafore, her hands clasped together, head tilted slightly as she answers shyly. Her small size is clear against the tall grass and the broad mushroom, and the two regard each other in a long silence, the Caterpillar's expression languid and stern, Alice's uncertain and apologetic.

moment.text: “Once upon a time there were three little sisters,” the Dormouse began in a great hurry; “and their names were Elsie, Lacie, and Tillie; and they lived at the bottom of a well—” “What did they live on?” said Alice, who always took a great interest in questions of eating and drinking. “They lived on treacle,” said the Dormouse, after thinking a minute or two. “They couldn’t have done that, you know,” Alice gently remarked; “they’d have been ill.” “So they were,” said the Dormouse; “_very_ ill.” Alice tried to fancy to herself what such an extraordinary way of living would be like, but it puzzled her too much, so she went on: “But why did they live at the bottom of a well?” “Take some more tea,” the March Hare said to Alice, very earnestly. “I’ve had nothing yet,” Alice replied in an offended tone, “so I can’t take more.” “You mean you can’t take _less_,” said the Hatter: “it’s very easy to take _more_ than nothing.” “Nobody asked _your_ opinion,” said Alice. “Who’s making personal remarks now?” the Hatter asked triumphantly. Alice did not quite know what to say to this: so she helped herself to some tea and bread-and-butter, and then turned to the Dormouse, and repeated her question. “Why did they live at the bottom of a well?”

On the raised bench the King of Hearts, in royal robes and crown, leans forward with a stern, considering face, while the Queen of Hearts sits beside him, one finger pointed accusingly toward the Knave of Hearts, who stands in the dock as a flat oblong card with head, arms and legs, his hands spread in innocent protest. In the jury box the jurymen in period waistcoats and hats look puzzled, their slates blank, and a few of them begin to brighten. moment.text: “It must be a very pretty dance,” said Alice timidly. “Would you like to see a little of it?” said the Mock Turtle. “Very much indeed,” said Alice. “Come, let’s try the first figure!” said the Mock Turtle to the Gryphon. “We can do without lobsters, you know. Which shall sing?” “Oh, _you_ sing,” said the Gryphon. “I’ve forgotten the words.” So they began solemnly dancing round and round Alice, every now and then treading on her toes when they passed too close, and waving their forepaws to mark the time, while the Mock Turtle sang this, very slowly and sadly:— “Will you walk a little faster?” said a whiting to a snail. “There’s a porpoise close behind us, and he’s treading on my tail. See how eagerly the lobsters and the turtles all advance! They are waiting on the shingle—will you come and join the dance? Will you, won’t you, will you, won’t you, will you join the dance? Will you, won’t you, will you, won’t you, won’t you join the dance? “You can really have no notion how delightful it will be When they take us up and throw us, with the lobsters, out to sea!” But the snail replied “Too far, too far!” and gave a look askance— Said he thanked the whiting kindly, but he would not join the dance. Would not, could not, would not, could not, would not join the dance. Would not, could not, would not, could not, could not join the dance. “What matters it how far we go?” his scaly friend replied. “There is another shore, you know, upon the other side. The further off from England the nearer is to France— Then turn not pale, beloved snail, but come and join the dance. Will you, won’t you, will you, won’t you, will you join the dance? Will you, won’t you, will you, won’t you, won’t you join the dance?”

moment.text: “Here!” cried Alice, quite forgetting in the flurry of the moment how large she had grown in the last few minutes, and she jumped up in such a hurry that she tipped over the jury-box with the edge of her skirt, upsetting all the jurymen on to the heads of the crowd below, and there they lay sprawling about, reminding her very much of a globe of goldfish she had accidentally upset the week before. “Oh, I _beg_ your pardon!” she exclaimed in a tone of great dismay, and began picking them up again as quickly as she could, for the accident of the goldfish kept running in her head, and she had a vague sort of idea that they must be collected at once and put back into the jury-box, or they would die. “The trial cannot proceed,” said the King in a very grave voice, “until all the jurymen are back in their proper places—_all_,” he repeated with great emphasis, looking hard at Alice as he said so. Alice looked at the jury-box, and saw that, in her haste, she had put the Lizard in head downwards, and the poor little thing was waving its tail about in a melancholy way, being quite unable to move. She soon got it out again, and put it right; “not that it signifies much,” she said to herself; “I should think it would be _quite_ as much use in the trial one way up as the other.”

next.text: As soon as the jury had a little recovered from the shock of being upset, and their slates and pencils had been found and handed back to them, they set to work very diligently to write out a history of the accident, all except the Lizard, who seemed too much overcome to do anything but sit with its mouth open, gazing up into the roof of the court.

plan.scene: Under a dawn sky shifting from dusk to morning, the wild dry Plain of the Jordan stretches out below, its mud-brick towns of Sodom and Gomorrah sitting on the flat land in the distance. A sulfurous haze hangs in the still air and smoke rises thickly from the plain. From the sky above the cities, fiery radiance and falling streams of burning sulfur and fire pour down onto the rooftops and walls, glowing orange through the smoke-filtered light. The towns are seen from a distance, with no figures in the foreground; a few scattered tents and trees on the edge of the dry land stand in silhouette against the glow. Light and smoke dominate the composition, rendering the destruction with restraint and without lingering gore, in a reverent and grounded mood.

plan.scene: At night, under a heavy sky and a strong east wind that drives sand and spray across the air, a long column of Israelites in woven tunics and cloaks walks steadily across a wide floor of dry, wind-rippled sand in the middle of the sea, carrying bundled belongings and leading their children and flocks. On their right and on their left, towering walls of water stand still and upright, their crests glimmering faintly where the spray catches the light. Above the column hangs a pillar of cloud glowing softly, and radiance spreads across the sea walls and the dry sand, with no figure visible. Near the front, Moses in a plain cloak stands at the edge of the path with his arm still lifted toward the water, his face turned toward the people. plan.scene: At the climax of the seventh day, under bright morning sunlight and dust rising from marching feet, the walls of Jericho are collapsing outward and flat, their stone ramparts and towers crumbling into great heaps at the base as billowing dust floods the air. Priests in linen garments stand near the front, raising ram's horn trumpets to their lips, their cheeks full with the sound. Ranks of Israelite men and women in woven tunics and cloaks press forward across the plain, shouting with great shouts, their arms raised, and surge straight ahead through the broken gaps where the wall has fallen, moving into the city. Joshua stands a little apart at the head of the people, one hand lifted, his cloak swept by the moving air. Beyond the breach, Canaanite townsfolk in plain undyed wool and linen stand frozen in startled stillness among the rubble, faces turned toward the noise. The light grows fuller and harsher as the day advances, casting short shadows across the broken stones and the dust-filled air.

plan.scene: Inside the dim stone lodging at the edge of Gibeah of Benjamin, late in the night, a single oil lamp and the last red embers of a hearth light the low room. The Levite stands at the center in an undyed ochre-brown woven wool tunic beneath a dusty grey-blue cloak, his back half turned toward the viewer, a knife held in one hand at his side and his other hand steadying the bundle of cloth on the floor. The concubine lies motionless on a woven mat near the wall, her body wrapped and partly bared at the edges, reduced to pale shapes that are restrained and not graphically shown; the cloth is laid out in careful, deliberate order. Around them stand earthen jars, a folded travel bag, a wooden donkey saddle leaning against the wall, and a bronze lamp stand. Cold blue moonlight enters through a narrow doorway and a small high window, pooling on the stone floor and mingling with the warm lamplight, while the grey beginning of dawn just touches the threshold. The mood is solemn, grave and quiet, the man's stillness expressing a terrible resolve rather than frenzy, with no spectacle, no blood pooling, and no lingering gore.

plan.scene: Late afternoon light falls warm and low across the mud-brick courtyard of a house in Bethlehem, where a stone threshold marks the open doorway onto a quiet village street. The air is clear and still with a faint evening haze. Inside the courtyard, a weathered wooden tablet-rack and a rolled scroll rest on a low stone bench, closed and unread, while a plain clay lamp burns with soft golden light. Nothing in the scene is an act of birth; the moment is one of quiet continuity, suggested by the stillness of the house, the lamplight, and the open door that looks outward toward the generations that will follow. plan.scene: At the instant the storm breaks off, Jesus stands upright in the stern of a small wooden fishing boat, one arm raised toward the water, his cloak pulled back by the last gusts of wind, his face calm and commanding. Around him the disciples crouch and cling to the gunwales and mast, soaked tunics clinging to their bodies, hands gripping ropes and the rail, faces turned toward him in awe and fear. A single oil lamp hangs swinging from the mast, its light catching the spray. The wind visibly ceases: the torn sail sags and hangs slack, and the rough, high-crested waves around the boat flatten into a glassy, still surface that reflects the pale silver light breaking through a parting of storm clouds. Distant rocky shoreline is faintly visible at the edge of the water, and the first hint of dawn tints the sky above the sea, which now lies perfectly calm and quiet.

plan.scene: At dawn on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, under a clear, calm sky with faint mist lifting off the water, Simon Peter, a broad-shouldered fisherman with a rough brown wool cloak gathered tightly about his body, leaps forward from a small wooden fishing boat and plunges into the shallows, the water splashing up in pale spray around his legs and chest. He has just stripped his cloak close around himself, one hand clutching its folds, his face turned toward the shore with eager urgency. In the boat behind him, the beloved disciple, a younger man in a wet linen tunic, stands at the gunwale pointing toward the beach, where a figure in a plain robe stands in the soft pale dawn light beside a charcoal fire glowing warmly on the stones at the water's edge. Around the boat the lake is still and silvery, and a heavy net of fish sags in the water beside the hull. Beyond the beach, low hills rise in the early light, and the first warm gold of the sun touches the surface of the lake.

plan.scene: In a single instant on a stone village road in Galilee, late afternoon light pours warm and golden from the west across a dusty track flanked by low stone walls and olive trees. The father, an older man in a simple undyed wool tunic and cloak, has reached his son at the edge of the road and has just gone down onto his knees in the dust; his arms are wrapped around the younger son's neck and shoulders and his head is bowed against him, so the father's face is turned away and only his bowed shape and the embrace are clear. The younger son, in a worn, dusty undyed tunic and cloak, with a worn traveling bag hanging from one shoulder and his sandals scuffed with the road, stands with his weight still half-yielded forward, his own arms lifting in hesitant return, his head bent in humility. Behind them the dust of the road hangs in a faint haze, catching the amber light, and beyond the wall the farmstead's olive trees cast long soft shadows over the courtyard gate, which stands half open. The air is clear and dry, the mood is tender and grounded, and the figures are shown with quiet dignity and without spectacle.

plan.scene: At the mouth of a rock-hewn tomb cut into a hillside outside Bethany, the great stone has been rolled aside and rests against the rock. Late afternoon sun slants low from the west across the rocky slope, while the cave interior stays dim, lit only by a single oil lamp set on a ledge. Jesus stands at the threshold, his head lifted and his arm extended toward the darkness, his mouth open in a loud call; he wears his dark blue-grey cloak, which the still, dry air hardly stirs. Within the shadowed opening, Lazarus is just emerging, upright and stepping forward, his body still wrapped in pale burial linen bindings at the hands, feet and face, the cloth loose and dusty. Martha stands close to the entrance, one hand pressed to her breast, her plain undyed tunic and head covering gray with dust, her face turned toward her brother in astonished hope. Behind them on the sloping ground a crowd of mourners in plain undyed tunics and cloaks stands gathered, some leaning forward, some with hands raised to their mouths, their figures softened by the warm light. A few pale clouds hang still over the hills and the air is clear and quiet, the moment charged with stillness before the bindings are loosed.

Ahead on the horizon, the pale stone walls and roofs of Damascus rise in the sunlit haze, quiet and ordinary, contrasting with the surge of light. plan.scene: In a stone village street at late afternoon, the low golden sun is just beginning to soften toward dusk, with a few high clouds drifting across a clear sky. Paul the apostle stands in the middle of the lane, wearing his canon attire of an ochre-brown tunic under a dark-blue cloak, one hand raised slightly as if in thoughtful address, his gaze lifted toward the open hillside beyond the village roofs. Around him, the rough stone houses and low walls catch the warm light on one side while the other side falls into cool blue shadow. A few townspeople in undyed wool tunics and cloaks pause at the edges of the street, some turning their heads toward him, while a Roman soldier in a plain cloak stands at the far edge of the town near the gate, observing without interfering. Beyond the village, a small fishing boat rests on a nearby shore, its sail furled, and the hillside stretches in open, quiet light. The scene conveys a moment of reflective hope, with the figures and surroundings calm and grounded under the fading sky.

plan.scene: Deep night in the open stone courtyard of the high priest's house in Jerusalem, lit by a warm orange glow from a charcoal brazier in the center. Dark stone walls rise around the yard, with a gate and passage at one side where faint pre-dawn grey begins to show at the edges of the sky. Simon Peter stands near the fire, a wool cloak drawn around his shoulders, his face turned sharply and his eyes wide with shock and recognition. A few figures in tunics and cloaks stand back in the shadows, half-turned away from him, and a Roman soldier in a cloak and helmet waits near the gate. Across the yard, in the passage, the figure of Jesus, bound and dignified, has turned his head and is looking directly at Peter through the firelight, his expression steady and sorrowful. The dark robes of priests are visible at the edge of the courtyard. The moment is still and heavy, with the smoke of the brazier drifting upward and the cool, quiet air of the night holding everything in suspense.

plan.scene: At Kadesh in the arid Wilderness of Zin, under a clear, hot, cloudless midday sky with strong bright desert sunlight casting hard, short shadows across pale rocky ground, Moses stands before a great outcrop of stone, lifting his arm high with his plain cloak falling from his shoulders and his rod raised in his hand as he strikes the rock. Water bursts forth from the stone in a sudden, abundant flow that glistens in the sunlight and spills across the dry ground. Beside him, Aaron, in white priestly linen, stands close and attentive, his face turned toward the water. Gathered in front of the rock, the Israelite people press forward in woven tunics and travelers' cloaks, some kneeling to cup the water in their hands, mothers lifting children, elders leaning on staffs, and their livestock, sheep and goats, drinking from the flow. Gathered tents of the camp stand at the edge of the scene under the same unshaded sun, and the whole gathering is shown in the single bright moment of midday with no change in the light.

plan.scene: In the warm mid-afternoon light of a stone courtyard outside the Jerusalem temple, beside the Beautiful Gate with its colonnade, Simon Peter kneels on the crowded steps and takes the right hand of a lame man who sits on the stone, lifting him upright with a firm, steady grip. The man's legs, long useless, are just beginning to bear weight, his feet pressing down onto the paving as his ankles straighten and gather strength. Beside Peter stands John, leaning in and watching the man closely with quiet attention. Around them the pilgrims and onlookers of the crowd step closer, some half-turned with wonder and some with hands raised, their tunics and cloaks catching the bright sunlight that falls across the stones and the broad steps of the temple. Behind them rise the temple's pale stone walls and gate columns under a clear, pale blue sky with a few light clouds, and on the outer walls a few Roman soldiers in military dress look down over the scene. The moment is held in stillness, the lifting of a body into life, with reverent astonishment spreading through the gathered crowd.

Short shadows pool beneath him on the sun-baked ground. Behind him the valley floor rises toward the Israelite and Philistine ridges, with distant soldiers in period armor visible but not in focus, and the cool dust of the brook bed contrasting with the hot, clear air. plan.scene: Inside the royal house at Gibeah, a stone-walled hall lit by warm oil lamps on a wooden lamp stand, dust hanging in the still, warm lamplight as evening deepens toward night. Saul, in a dark royal tunic and cloak, rises from his seat in mid-throw, his arm flung back and a bronze-headed spear leaving his hand toward the tall wall behind where David stands. David, in a plain shepherd's tunic, has ducked and turned aside, his body twisting out of the spear's path while his harp lies abandoned on the floor near his feet. The spear's shaft cuts a diagonal through the lamplight and strikes the stone wall beside him. A faint, restless haze drifts through the upper hall, dim and unformed, stirring the flames of the lamps so they flicker and bend, the only sign of the presence that has come upon the king. Light falls warm across the stone, the figures of the king and the young man caught in the tense instant of escape.

plan.scene: In a Bethlehem house courtyard of stone walls and an open threshold, late afternoon light slants low and golden through the gate, softening toward dusk-blue shadows under a clear, dry sky with a faint warm haze. Samuel, in a long undyed linen tunic belted under a deep blue wool cloak, stands at the center, lifting a small horn of oil as he pours it over the head of David, a young man with ruddy skin and a handsome, steady face, who kneels before him in an earth-toned tunic and cloak. Around them the brothers stand in a loose half-circle: Eliab tall and stern-faced, Abinadab and Shammah watching with quiet attention, and Jesse at the edge near the doorway, his hands folded and his expression grave. Clay vessels and a stone bench sit against the wall, and the oil glints faintly in the fading light. The air above them carries a faint radiance, suggested by a soft brightness around David that hints at the Spirit of Yahweh coming upon him, while the courtyard lies still and reverent.

plan.scene: In the royal banquet hall of the palace of Babylon at night, warm lamplight and torch glow from wall sconces flicker gold across polished vessels, glazed blue tiles and tall columns, while deep shadow gathers at the edges. Belshazzar sits on a raised couch at the head of a long table laden with gold cups and half-eaten feasts, dressed in an embroidered royal tunic with a jeweled collar and a rich cloak, one hand lifted in a dismissive gesture as he turns toward the man before him. Daniel stands upright in the open floor below the dais, calm and unhurried, wearing his indigo wool cloak with its blue fringed hem over a plain tunic, his bearing dignified rather than defiant. Nearby, a few courtiers in court robes shift uneasily at the tables, their faces half turned toward the king and the prophet. A pale scroll lies rolled on a side table near the king's couch, its contents unseen. The air is still and warm, the feast interrupted, and the moment hangs in tense quiet as Daniel speaks his refusal of the rewards and prepares to answer the king.

plan.scene: In the royal banquet hall of the palace of Babylon at night, warm lamplight and torch glow from wall sconces flicker gold across polished vessels, glazed blue tiles and tall columns, while deep shadow gathers at the edges. Belshazzar sits on a raised couch at the head of a long table laden with gold cups and half-eaten feasts, dressed in an embroidered royal tunic with a jeweled collar and a rich cloak, one hand lifted in a dismissive gesture as he turns toward the man before him. Daniel stands upright in the open floor below the dais, calm and unhurried, wearing his indigo wool cloak with its blue fringed hem over a plain tunic, his bearing dignified rather than defiant. Nearby, a few courtiers in court robes shift uneasily at the tables, their faces half turned toward the king and the prophet. A pale scroll lies rolled on a side table near the king's couch, its contents unseen. The air is still and warm, the feast interrupted, and the moment hangs in tense quiet as Daniel speaks his refusal of the rewards and prepares to answer the king.

plan.scene: At the mouth of a rough-hewn stone den beneath a royal palace in Babylon, the dawn light has just begun to spill softly through the opening, while torches and lamps still burn low against the dark stone walls. Within the pit, the floor is sandy and bare, with no plants growing in it, and the lions lie quiet and unthreatening at the far edges, their great heads lowered. Daniel, in a plain linen tunic and cloak, has been drawn up by ropes and stands at the edge of the pit, unhurt, his arms relaxed at his sides and his face calm and turned upward with quiet trust. Darius the Mede, in royal court robes with a fine mantle, leans forward at the sealed entrance stone, his hands open in gladness and relief as attendants steady the ropes around Daniel. plan.scene: At night under a violent storm, dark clouds tear across a moonlit sky as high waves of the Sea of Galilee crash against a small fishing boat, its hull already half-filled with water. Wind whips soaked tunics and cloaks, and spray hangs in the air. In the stern, Jesus lies asleep on a cushion, wrapped in a cloak, his body calm amid the chaos. Several disciples cling to the gunwales and bail frantically with wooden buckets, faces drawn with fear. One disciple leans over the stern, grasping Jesus's shoulder and turning toward him with an anguished, pleading expression, while the others brace against the tilting deck. Dim silver moonlight breaks through in patches on the churning water, and a distant rocky shoreline is faintly visible through the spray. Oil lamps are unlit; the scene is lit only by the moon and the pale glow of breaking waves.

plan.scene: In a stone audience chamber of the Jerusalem palace, late afternoon, low golden light slanting across the stone floor through high windows and a faint haze of distant dust hanging in the dry air. Hanani the seer stands before the throne in a plain undyed cloak, one hand raised with open palm toward the king, his face grave and steady rather than wrathful. King Asa sits on his throne in court robes, leaning forward with his hands gripping the armrests, his expression caught between surprise and unease. Behind Hanani, a pale radiance of light and cloud gathers faintly against the far wall, suggesting the watching eyes of Yahweh moving across the earth without showing any human form. Two guards in period armor stand at the doorway, bronze helmets catching the warm light, their spears held upright and their eyes lowered. Through the open window behind the throne, the city of Jerusalem spreads in golden stone and shadow, with the faint outline of the temple's priestly linen visible in the distance and the frontier hills fading into the hazy dusk. Unrolled scroll on a side table, blank and closed, is not read.

plan.scene: On the bare ash heap outside a village, under a wide open sky with thin high cloud and still, dry air, late afternoon sun lays warm amber light from the west and throws long soft shadows across the scattered grey ash. Job stands near the heap's edge, a little hunched, his body held tight against the dread that has seized him; his hands are half-raised, fingers curled as if warding off something coming toward him from the open ground. He wears his canonical deep indigo wool cloak, dusted with ash along its hem and shoulders, over a plain tunic darkened by the dust of the heap. His face is turned slightly away from the sun, toward the distant road, and his posture shows fear and anguish pressing on him from every side, like an army of troubles closing in, though no other figure is present. Around him the ash lies scattered and grey, a few broken clay vessels half-buried in it, and the dry earth shows fine cracks where the wind has swept it bare. The mood is grave and still, with nothing violent in view, only the heavy quiet of a man overwhelmed by sorrow on a mourner's ground.

plan.scene: In a sunlit stone courtyard of a synagogue in a Roman-ruled Judean town, under clear, dry daytime air and warm, even Mediterranean light with soft haze, Paul the apostle stands in a plain wool cloak over a tunic, one hand raised in a steady, teaching gesture, his face turned toward a small gathering of men and women from both Jewish and Gentile households. Some hold rolled scrolls closed at their sides, and a few stand in gentle shadow cast by the stone archway. Beyond the low courtyard wall, the rooftops and white walls of a Gentile city rise under the same open sky, with a Roman soldier in military dress passing along a distant road. Nobody in the scene is blindfolded or being led; the image is of Paul as a confident guide and lamp, his posture open and assured, with a single oil lamp set on a stone ledge beside him giving warm light to the faces turned toward him, the listeners' expressions attentive and dignified rather than dramatic.

In the center, a king in a court robe stands gazing upward toward the high window, his face in thoughtful stillness, as the low sun lights the upper walls and the lower hall stays in soft shadow, suggesting heights and depths beyond reach. Around him, members of the court in linen tunics and scribes' mantles stand at a respectful distance, some looking toward the king, others lowering their eyes. In the alcove, two men of Hezekiah's household sit at a low table, a rolled scroll closed beside them and a reed pen resting, one hand paused over the scroll as they listen and reflect. plan.scene: In a stone village courtyard in Roman Judea, early evening, the last of the daylight fading into amber lamplight. A young man in a plain tunic and wool cloak stands at the threshold of a simple stone house, turning back slightly as an older man and woman, his father and mother, stand near the doorway with their hands resting gently on his shoulders in parting. Across the open courtyard a young woman in a simple white wedding veil and fringed mantle waits beside a low wall, her face lifted toward him, the two of them reaching toward each other across the warm dusk air. Oil lamps glow in the windows of the house, casting soft light on the packed earth and the stone walls; in the distance a synagogue's plain roofline stands against the deepening blue sky. The air is still and clear, and the figures are shown in the act of leaving and joining, the moment where two households become one.

plan.scene: On the banks of the river Ulai beneath a night sky thinning into the first pale gold of dawn, Daniel stands in a plain tunic and cloak at the water's edge, his face turned toward the figure beside him. The man clothed in linen, wearing priestly linen, stands calm and upright on the riverbank, one hand lifted toward the far shore as if pointing out a vision. The river Ulai flows still and dark, its surface catching the cool moonlight, and thin cloud banks drift slowly above it under a faint radiance from the heavens. Across the water, the distant outline of a fortified city wall rises against the sky, and in the dim foreground a loose gathering of armed men in period armor stirs restlessly in the half-light, their spears and shields raised in the gesture of rival factions rising against one another. Their stance suggests conflict rising but not yet joined. The scene is quiet and reverent, with the mood of grief and solemn expectation, and the light slowly warms from silver toward gold as the section moves toward morning.

Saul, in his royal court robe of rich cloth, has lunged forward and seized the hem of Samuel's garment in his fist, and the fabric is tearing at the skirt, the rip running open in the moment of pulling. Israelite men and women in woven tunics and cloaks pause in the open ground between tents, some with bundles of gold rings and cloth slipping from their arms, turning toward Moses with calm, attentive faces as they set their offerings down on a growing heap of goods near the court entrance. Behind them, craftsmen in leather work aprons stand beside a half-raised framework of acacia boards and a bronze laver, their tools laid still on a low bench in the dry, hazy sunlight and soft shadows cast under the tent awnings. plan.scene: On an open stadium track in a Roman-era Mediterranean city, late afternoon sunlight falls warm and golden from the low west, casting long soft shadows across the packed red earth. Stone seating tiers rise on one side, crowded with a great throng of onlookers in simple tunics and cloaks, their faces turned toward the track in quiet expectation, while beyond the stands the distant sea glimmers and hills rest under a clear sky with scattered high clouds. In the foreground a single runner in plain athletic wear and sandals bends forward at the start, one hand brushing aside a loose cloak and a heavy pack slipping from his shoulder onto the ground, shedding weight as he readies to press on. moment.reference: A Scandal in Bohemia, Part I ¶1
moment.text: To Sherlock Holmes she is always _the_ woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

next.text: I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

plan.scene: Holmes sits alone in his lamplit sitting room at 221B Baker Street, in shirtsleeves and waistcoat, his long frame sunk into a worn armchair beside the coal fire. He holds a sheet of folded correspondence loosely in one hand, his gaze fixed on the low flames and his face composed and inward, as though weighing a problem rather than a sentiment. The desk behind him is crowded with papers, a chemical retort and a pipe rack, and the bookshelves hold rows of dark volumes. Beyond the drawn curtains, damp London fog presses against the window panes, softening the glow of the distant gas lamps. The room is warm and dim, with firelight and lamplight pooling across the rug and the scattered books, and the atmosphere is one of restrained, solitary concentration.

plan.scene: Holmes sits alone in his lamplit sitting room at 221B Baker Street, in shirtsleeves and waistcoat, his long frame sunk into a worn armchair beside the coal fire. He holds a sheet of folded correspondence loosely in one hand, his gaze fixed on the low flames and his face composed and inward, as though weighing a problem rather than a sentiment. The desk behind him is crowded with papers, a chemical retort and a pipe rack, and the bookshelves hold rows of dark volumes. Beyond the drawn curtains, damp London fog presses against the window panes, softening the glow of the distant gas lamps. The room is warm and dim, with firelight and lamplight pooling across the rug and the scattered books, and the atmosphere is one of restrained, solitary concentration.

moment.text: I had called upon my friend, Mr. Sherlock Holmes, one day in the autumn of last year and found him in deep conversation with a very stout, florid-faced, elderly gentleman with fiery red hair. With an apology for my intrusion, I was about to withdraw when Holmes pulled me abruptly into the room and closed the door behind me. “You could not possibly have come at a better time, my dear Watson,” he said cordially. “I was afraid that you were engaged.” “So I am. Very much so.” “Then I can wait in the next room.” “Not at all. This gentleman, Mr. Wilson, has been my partner and helper in many of my most successful cases, and I have no doubt that he will be of the utmost use to me in yours also.” The stout gentleman half rose from his chair and gave a bob of greeting, with a quick little questioning glance from his small fat-encircled eyes.

next.text: “Try the settee,” said Holmes, relapsing into his armchair and putting his fingertips together, as was his custom when in judicial moods. “I know, my dear Watson, that you share my love of all that is bizarre and outside the conventions and humdrum routine of everyday life. You have shown your relish for it by the enthusiasm which has prompted you to chronicle, and, if you will excuse my saying so, somewhat to embellish so many of my own little adventures.”

moment.text: As he spoke there was the sharp sound of horses’ hoofs and grating wheels against the curb, followed by a sharp pull at the bell. Holmes whistled. “A pair, by the sound,” said he. “Yes,” he continued, glancing out of the window. “A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties. A hundred and fifty guineas apiece. There’s money in this case, Watson, if there is nothing else.” “I think that I had better go, Holmes.” “Not a bit, Doctor. Stay where you are. I am lost without my Boswell. And this promises to be interesting. It would be a pity to miss it.” “But your client—” “Never mind him. I may want your help, and so may he. Here he comes. Sit down in that armchair, Doctor, and give us your best attention.” A slow and heavy step, which had been heard upon the stairs and in the passage, paused immediately outside the door. Then there was a loud and authoritative tap. “Come in!” said Holmes. A man entered who could hardly have been less than six feet six inches in height, with the chest and limbs of a Hercules. His dress was rich with a richness which would, in England, be looked upon as akin to bad taste. Heavy bands of astrakhan were slashed across the sleeves and fronts of his double-breasted coat, while the deep blue cloak which was thrown over his shoulders was lined with flame-coloured silk and secured at the neck with a brooch which consisted of a single flaming beryl. Boots which extended halfway up his calves, and which were trimmed at the tops with rich brown fur, completed the impression of barbaric opulence which was suggested by his whole appearance. He carried a broad-brimmed hat in his hand, while he wore across the upper part of his face, extending down past the cheekbones, a black vizard mask, which he had apparently adjusted that very moment, for his hand was still raised to it as he entered. From the lower part of the face he appeared to be a man of strong character, with a thick, hanging lip, and a long, straight chin suggestive of resolution pushed to the length of obstinacy. “You had my note?” he asked with a deep harsh voice and a strongly marked German accent. “I told you that I would call.” He looked from one to the other of us, as if uncertain which to address. “Pray take a seat,” said Holmes. “This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, who is occasionally good enough to help me in my cases. Whom have I the honour to address?” “You may address me as the Count Von Kramm, a Bohemian nobleman. I understand that this gentleman, your friend, is a man of honour and discretion, whom I may trust with a matter of the most extreme importance. If not, I should much prefer to communicate with you alone.” I rose to go, but Holmes caught me by the wrist and pushed me back into my chair. “It is both, or none,” said he. “You may say before this gentleman anything which you may say to me.” The Count shrugged his broad shoulders. “Then I must begin,” said he, “by binding you both to absolute secrecy for two years; at the end of that time the matter will be of no importance. At present it is not too much to say that it is of such weight it may have an influence upon European history.”

moment.text: “Which surely he restored to their owner?” “My dear fellow, there lies the problem. It is true that ‘For Mrs. Henry Baker’ was printed upon a small card which was tied to the bird’s left leg, and it is also true that the initials ‘H. B.’ are legible upon the lining of this hat, but as there are some thousands of Bakers, and some hundreds of Henry Bakers in this city of ours, it is not easy to restore lost property to any one of them.” “What, then, did Peterson do?” “He brought round both hat and goose to me on Christmas morning, knowing that even the smallest problems are of interest to me. The goose we retained until this morning, when there were signs that, in spite of the slight frost, it would be well that it should be eaten without unnecessary delay. Its finder has carried it off, therefore, to fulfil the ultimate destiny of a goose, while I continue to retain the hat of the unknown gentleman who lost his Christmas dinner.” “Did he not advertise?” “No.” “Then, what clue could you have as to his identity?” “Only as much as we can deduce.” “From his hat?” “Precisely.” “But you are joking. What can you gather from this old battered felt?” “Here is my lens. You know my methods. What can you gather yourself as to the individuality of the man who has worn this article?”

moment.text: We travelled by the Underground as far as Aldersgate; and a short walk took us to Saxe-Coburg Square, the scene of the singular story which we had listened to in the morning. It was a poky, little, shabby-genteel place, where four lines of dingy two-storied brick houses looked out into a small railed-in enclosure, where a lawn of weedy grass and a few clumps of faded laurel bushes made a hard fight against a smoke-laden and uncongenial atmosphere. Three gilt balls and a brown board with “JABEZ WILSON” in white letters, upon a corner house, announced the place where our red-headed client carried on his business. Sherlock Holmes stopped in front of it with his head on one side and looked it all over, with his eyes shining brightly between puckered lids. Then he walked slowly up the street, and then down again to the corner, still looking keenly at the houses. Finally he returned to the pawnbroker’s, and, having thumped vigorously upon the pavement with his stick two or three times, he went up to the door and knocked. It was instantly opened by a bright-looking, clean-shaven young fellow, who asked him to step in. “Thank you,” said Holmes, “I only wished to ask you how you would go from here to the Strand.” “Third right, fourth left,” answered the assistant promptly, closing the door. “Smart fellow, that,” observed Holmes as we walked away. “He is, in my judgment, the fourth smartest man in London, and for daring I am not sure that he has not a claim to be third. I have known something of him before.” “Evidently,” said I, “Mr. Wilson’s assistant counts for a good deal in this mystery of the Red-headed League. I am sure that you inquired your way merely in order that you might see him.” “Not him.” “What then?” “The knees of his trousers.” “And what did you see?” “What I expected to see.” “Why did you beat the pavement?” “My dear doctor, this is a time for observation, not for talk. We are spies in an enemy’s country. We know something of Saxe-Coburg Square. Let us now explore the parts which lie behind it.”

previous.text: “Then put on your hat and come. I am going through the City first, and we can have some lunch on the way. I observe that there is a good deal of German music on the programme, which is rather more to my taste than Italian or French. It is introspective, and I want to introspect. Come along!”

next.text: The road in which we found ourselves as we turned round the corner from the retired Saxe-Coburg Square presented as great a contrast to it as the front of a picture does to the back. It was one of the main arteries which conveyed the traffic of the City to the north and west. The roadway was blocked with the immense stream of commerce flowing in a double tide inward and outward, while the footpaths were black with the hurrying swarm of pedestrians. It was difficult to realise as we looked at the line of fine shops and stately business premises that they really abutted on the other side upon the faded and stagnant square which we had just quitted.

moment.text: “You are not very vulnerable from above,” Holmes remarked as he held up the lantern and gazed about him. “Nor from below,” said Mr. Merryweather, striking his stick upon the flags which lined the floor. “Why, dear me, it sounds quite hollow!” he remarked, looking up in surprise. “I must really ask you to be a little more quiet!” said Holmes severely. “You have already imperilled the whole success of our expedition. Might I beg that you would have the goodness to sit down upon one of those boxes, and not to interfere?” The solemn Mr. Merryweather perched himself upon a crate, with a very injured expression upon his face, while Holmes fell upon his knees upon the floor and, with the lantern and a magnifying lens, began to examine minutely the cracks between the stones. A few seconds sufficed to satisfy him, for he sprang to his feet again and put his glass in his pocket. “We have at least an hour before us,” he remarked, “for they can hardly take any steps until the good pawnbroker is safely in bed. Then they will not lose a minute, for the sooner they do their work the longer time they will have for their escape. We are at present, Doctor—as no doubt you have divined—in the cellar of the City branch of one of the principal London banks. Mr. Merryweather is the chairman of directors, and he will explain to you that there are reasons why the more daring criminals of London should take a considerable interest in this cellar at present.” “It is our French gold,” whispered the director. “We have had several warnings that an attempt might be made upon it.” “Your French gold?” “Yes. We had occasion some months ago to strengthen our resources and borrowed for that purpose 30,000 napoleons from the Bank of France. It has become known that we have never had occasion to unpack the money, and that it is still lying in our cellar. The crate upon which I sit contains 2,000 napoleons packed between layers of lead foil. Our reserve of bullion is much larger at present than is usually kept in a single branch office, and the directors have had misgivings upon the subject.”

next.text: “Which were very well justified,” observed Holmes. “And now it is time that we arranged our little plans. I expect that within an hour matters will come to a head. In the meantime Mr. Merryweather, we must put the screen over that dark lantern.”

moment.text: From outside came the occasional cry of a night-bird, and once at our very window a long drawn catlike whine, which told us that the cheetah was indeed at liberty. Far away we could hear the deep tones of the parish clock, which boomed out every quarter of an hour. How long they seemed, those quarters! Twelve struck, and one and two and three, and still we sat waiting silently for whatever might befall. Suddenly there was the momentary gleam of a light up in the direction of the ventilator, which vanished immediately, but was succeeded by a strong smell of burning oil and heated metal. Someone in the next room had lit a dark-lantern. I heard a gentle sound of movement, and then all was silent once more, though the smell grew stronger. For half an hour I sat with straining ears. Then suddenly another sound became audible—a very gentle, soothing sound, like that of a small jet of steam escaping continually from a kettle. The instant that we heard it, Holmes sprang from the bed, struck a match, and lashed furiously with his cane at the bell-pull. “You see it, Watson?” he yelled. “You see it?” But I saw nothing. At the moment when Holmes struck the light I heard a low, clear whistle, but the sudden glare flashing into my weary eyes made it impossible for me to tell what it was at which my friend lashed so savagely. I could, however, see that his face was deadly pale and filled with horror and loathing. He had ceased to strike and was gazing up at the ventilator when suddenly there broke from the silence of the night the most horrible cry to which I have ever listened. It swelled up louder and louder, a hoarse yell of pain and fear and anger all mingled in the one dreadful shriek. They say that away down in the village, and even in the distant parsonage, that cry raised the sleepers from their beds. It struck cold to our hearts, and I stood gazing at Holmes, and he at me, until the last echoes of it had died away into the silence from which it rose. “What can it mean?” I gasped. “It means that it is all over,” Holmes answered. “And perhaps, after all, it is for the best. Take your pistol, and we will enter Dr. Roylott’s room.”

moment.text: “Which were very well justified,” observed Holmes. “And now it is time that we arranged our little plans. I expect that within an hour matters will come to a head. In the meantime Mr. Merryweather, we must put the screen over that dark lantern.” “And sit in the dark?” “I am afraid so. I had brought a pack of cards in my pocket, and I thought that, as we were a _partie carrée_, you might have your rubber after all. But I see that the enemy’s preparations have gone so far that we cannot risk the presence of a light. And, first of all, we must choose our positions. These are daring men, and though we shall take them at a disadvantage, they may do us some harm unless we are careful. I shall stand behind this crate, and do you conceal yourselves behind those. Then, when I flash a light upon them, close in swiftly. If they fire, Watson, have no compunction about shooting them down.” I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case behind which I crouched. Holmes shot the slide across the front of his lantern and left us in pitch darkness—such an absolute darkness as I have never before experienced. The smell of hot metal remained to assure us that the light was still there, ready to flash out at a moment’s notice. To me, with my nerves worked up to a pitch of expectancy, there was something depressing and subduing in the sudden gloom, and in the cold dank air of the vault. “They have but one retreat,” whispered Holmes. “That is back through the house into Saxe-Coburg Square. I hope that you have done what I asked you, Jones?” “I have an inspector and two officers waiting at the front door.” “Then we have stopped all the holes. And now we must be silent and wait.” What a time it seemed! From comparing notes afterwards it was but an hour and a quarter, yet it appeared to me that the night must have almost gone, and the dawn be breaking above us. My limbs were weary and stiff, for I feared to change my position; yet my nerves were worked up to the highest pitch of tension, and my hearing was so acute that I could not only hear the gentle breathing of my companions, but I could distinguish the deeper, heavier in-breath of the bulky Jones from the thin, sighing note of the bank director. From my position I could look over the case in the direction of the floor. Suddenly my eyes caught the glint of a light.

Our reserve of bullion is much larger at present than is usually kept in a single branch office, and the directors have had misgivings upon the subject.”

moment.text: We had the carriage to ourselves save for an immense litter of papers which Holmes had brought with him. Among these he rummaged and read, with intervals of note-taking and of meditation, until we were past Reading. Then he suddenly rolled them all into a gigantic ball and tossed them up onto the rack. “Have you heard anything of the case?” he asked. “Not a word. I have not seen a paper for some days.” “The London press has not had very full accounts. I have just been looking through all the recent papers in order to master the particulars. It seems, from what I gather, to be one of those simple cases which are so extremely difficult.” “That sounds a little paradoxical.” “But it is profoundly true. Singularity is almost invariably a clue. The more featureless and commonplace a crime is, the more difficult it is to bring it home. In this case, however, they have established a very serious case against the son of the murdered man.” “It is a murder, then?” “Well, it is conjectured to be so. I shall take nothing for granted until I have the opportunity of looking personally into it. I will explain the state of things to you, as far as I have been able to understand it, in a very few words.

moment.text: But the inspector was mistaken, for those criminals were not destined to fall into the hands of justice. As we rolled into Eyford Station we saw a gigantic column of smoke which streamed up from behind a small clump of trees in the neighbourhood and hung like an immense ostrich feather over the landscape. “A house on fire?” asked Bradstreet as the train steamed off again on its way. “Yes, sir!” said the station-master. “When did it break out?” “I hear that it was during the night, sir, but it has got worse, and the whole place is in a blaze.”

moment.text: “I’ve wasted time enough,” said Lestrade, rising. “I believe in hard work and not in sitting by the fire spinning fine theories. Good-day, Mr. Holmes, and we shall see which gets to the bottom of the matter first.” He gathered up the garments, thrust them into the bag, and made for the door. “Just one hint to you, Lestrade,” drawled Holmes before his rival vanished; “I will tell you the true solution of the matter. Lady St. Simon is a myth. There is not, and there never has been, any such person.” Lestrade looked sadly at my companion. moment.text: “It was naturally my intention that he should succeed me in my business, but he was not of a business turn. He was wild, wayward, and, to speak the truth, I could not trust him in the handling of large sums of money. When he was young he became a member of an aristocratic club, and there, having charming manners, he was soon the intimate of a number of men with long purses and expensive habits. He learned to play heavily at cards and to squander money on the turf, until he had again and again to come to me and implore me to give him an advance upon his allowance, that he might settle his debts of honour. He tried more than once to break away from the dangerous company which he was keeping, but each time the influence of his friend, Sir George Burnwell, was enough to draw him back again. “And, indeed, I could not wonder that such a man as Sir George Burnwell should gain an influence over him, for he has frequently brought him to my house, and I have found myself that I could hardly resist the fascination of his manner. He is older than Arthur, a man of the world to his finger-tips, one who had been everywhere, seen everything, a brilliant talker, and a man of great personal beauty. Yet when I think of him in cold blood, far away from the glamour of his presence, I am convinced from his cynical speech and the look which I have caught in his eyes that he is one who should be deeply distrusted. So I think, and so, too, thinks my little Mary, who has a woman’s quick insight into character. “And now there is only she to be described. She is my niece; but when my brother died five years ago and left her alone in the world I adopted her, and have looked upon her ever since as my daughter. She is a sunbeam in my house—sweet, loving, beautiful, a wonderful manager and housekeeper, yet as tender and quiet and gentle as a woman could be. She is my right hand. I do not know what I could do without her. In only one matter has she ever gone against my wishes. Twice my boy has asked her to marry him, for he loves her devotedly, but each time she has refused him. I think that if anyone could have drawn him into the right path it would have been she, and that his marriage might have changed his whole life; but now, alas! it is too late—forever too late! “Now, Mr. Holmes, you know the people who live under my roof, and I shall continue with my miserable story. “When we were taking coffee in the drawing-room that night after dinner, I told Arthur and Mary my experience, and of the precious treasure which we had under our roof, suppressing only the name of my client. Lucy Parr, who had brought in the coffee, had, I am sure, left the room; but I cannot swear that the door was closed. Mary and Arthur were much interested and wished to see the famous coronet, but I thought it better not to disturb it. “‘Where have you put it?’ asked Arthur. “‘In my own bureau.’ “‘Well, I hope to goodness the house won’t be burgled during the night.’ said he. “‘It is locked up,’ I answered. “‘Oh, any old key will fit that bureau. When I was a youngster I have opened it myself with the key of the box-room cupboard.’ “He often had a wild way of talking, so that I thought little of what he said. He followed me to my room, however, that night with a very grave face.

previous.text: “So much for the servants. My family itself is so small that it will not take me long to describe it. I am a widower and have an only son, Arthur. He has been a disappointment to me, Mr. Holmes—a grievous disappointment. I have no doubt that I am myself to blame. People tell me that I have spoiled him. Very likely I have. When my dear wife died I felt that he was all I had to love. I could not bear to see the smile fade even for a moment from his face. I have never denied him a wish. Perhaps it would have been better for both of us had I been sterner, but I meant it for the best.
